topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines unit labour cost?
options: Labour cost per unit of output, combining the wage rate with productivity
The hourly wage paid to a production worker
The total wage bill of a business
The cost of training a new employee
questions.why: This is the figure that matters in a location decision, not the wage rate on its own.
whyNot: That is the wage rate, only one half of the calculation.
That is the total labour cost.
That is a recruitment cost.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a special economic zone?
options: An area within a country where trade, tax and regulatory rules are relaxed to attract investment
A region where only domestic firms may operate
A country that has joined a trading bloc
An area reserved for agricultural production
questions.why: Zones are one form of government incentive, alongside grants, tax holidays and subsidised sites.
whyNot: Zones are designed to attract foreign investment, not exclude it.
That is bloc membership.
That is land-use zoning.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a footloose business?
options: A business with no strong tie to a particular location, which can relocate relatively easily
A business that operates only in its home country
A business that has recently been established
A business with a large number of employees
questions.why: Where investment is genuinely mobile, such as assembly or service centres, the threat to relocate gives the business real bargaining power.
whyNot: That is a domestic business.
Age does not determine mobility.
Size does not determine mobility.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines return on investment?
options: The profit expected from an investment expressed as a percentage of the amount invested
The time taken for an investment to repay its cost
The total revenue an investment generates
The interest rate charged on the loan funding an investment
questions.why: It should be compared with the alternative locations and with the business's cost of capital.
whyNot: That is the payback period.
Revenue is not a return measure.
That is the cost of finance.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Country A pays $4.00 per hour with output of 2 units per hour. What is its unit labour cost?
whyNot: That multiplies rather than divides.
That is the hourly wage.
That inverts the calculation.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Country B pays $18.00 per hour with output of 12 units per hour. What is its unit labour cost?
questions.why: 18.00 / 12 = $1.50 per unit, which is lower than Country A's $2.00 despite a wage more than four times higher.
whyNot: That multiplies rather than divides.
That is the hourly wage.
That inverts the calculation.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Unit labour cost is $2.00, shipping $0.60 and tariff $0.96 per unit. What is the delivered cost of those elements?
questions.why: 2.00 + 0.60 + 0.96 = $3.56 per unit, which is what should be compared between locations.
whyNot: That omits the tariff.
That omits the shipping cost.
That omits the labour cost.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why should government incentives tip a decision rather than make it?
options: They are usually time-limited, so the advantage expires while the plant remains
They are always illegal under WTO rules
They are never actually paid
They apply only to domestic businesses
questions.why: They can also be withdrawn by a new government, and a location that has to pay businesses to come is telling you something about its other disadvantages.
whyNot: Investment incentives are widely used and generally lawful.
They are normally paid as agreed.
They are typically aimed at inward investors.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which factor is most decisive for capital-intensive manufacturing?
options: Power reliability and infrastructure
The minimum wage rate
Local consumer incomes
The number of competitors in the market
questions.why: A plant that stops when the supply fails either needs its own generation or loses output, and wages matter far less where labour is a small share of cost.
whyNot: Wages matter most for labour-intensive production.
Consumer incomes matter for a market assessment.
Competitor numbers affect the market, not the location.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Which factor most often defeats a location decision that looks attractive on cost?
options: Skill shortages, because training takes years
The exchange rate on the day of the decision
The colour of the national flag on packaging
The number of public holidays
questions.why: Where the business needs a skill nobody local has, the choice is to train, to import expatriate staff at high cost, or to go elsewhere.
whyNot: A single day's rate is not a structural factor.
That is not a serious consideration.
Holidays are a minor operational detail.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why must rules of origin be checked when locating inside a free trade area?
options: Assembling from components made outside may not qualify for tariff-free treatment
Free trade areas prohibit foreign ownership of factories
Free trade areas require a single currency
Rules of origin determine the local minimum wage
questions.why: A stated proportion of the value usually has to originate within the bloc, which is why a customs union removes the problem.
whyNot: Foreign ownership is generally permitted.
A single currency belongs to a monetary union.
Wages are set nationally.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why might a business require a higher return from a location in an unstable country?
options: The range of possible outcomes is wider, so a risk premium is appropriate
Unstable countries always have higher tax rates
Returns are calculated differently in unstable countries
Investors are legally required to demand more
questions.why: A higher expected return in an unstable country may be worth less than a lower return in a stable one.
whyNot: Tax rates vary independently of stability.
The calculation is the same; the required return differs.
No such legal requirement exists.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why is processing close to a natural resource often chosen?
options: It saves transport cost on waste material that would otherwise be shipped
Resource-rich countries always offer the lowest wages
Processing is prohibited in consuming countries
It removes the need for any infrastructure
questions.why: It is decisive for extractive and processing industries, and important wherever a bulky raw material is a large share of cost.
whyNot: Wage levels vary independently of resource endowment.
Processing is widely done in consuming countries too.
Processing requires substantial infrastructure.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: What should be the first sentence of a location assessment answer?
options: An identification of what kind of production this is, so the factors can be ranked
A statement of the recommendation
A definition of foreign direct investment
A list of all nine location factors
questions.why: Location factors are only meaningful relative to what the business actually does, so a generic list in a fixed order cannot reach the top band.
whyNot: A recommendation before analysis is unsupported.
A definition adds little to a location judgement.
An unranked list is the weakest possible structure.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why does a location with very low wages sometimes lose out to a high-wage one?
options: Productivity, transport cost and tariffs can more than offset the wage advantage
High wages always indicate better product quality
Low-wage countries prohibit foreign investment
Tariffs are only charged on low-wage exports
questions.why: This is exactly why high-wage economies retain capital-intensive production.
whyNot: Quality depends on process and skills, not on wages directly.
Most low-wage countries actively seek foreign investment.
Tariffs depend on the product and route, not the exporter's wage level.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: For a service operation, which factors matter most?
options: Language, education, telecommunications and time zone
Port capacity and cold-chain facilities
Proximity to mineral deposits
Road access for heavy vehicles
questions.why: The relevant factors follow from what the business actually does, which is the organising idea of this topic.
whyNot: Those matter for physical goods, particularly perishables.
That matters for extractive industries.
That matters for bulky physical output.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a production location
questions.stem: Why can a country be a poor production location and an excellent place to sell services?
options: The same factors produce opposite answers depending on what the business does
Service businesses are exempt from location factors
Production locations are chosen by governments
Services do not require any workforce
questions.why: A manufacturer would not locate in a small remote island economy and a resort operator would, on the same set of factors.
whyNot: They apply to services too, just with different weights.
Businesses choose their own locations.
Services are often highly labour-intensive.
